title: Draw the trusted computing base
objective: Mark each component of your system as proved, validated per run, tested or trusted, and sort a claim into the command, the compiler or the runtime.

blocks.md: Every proof in this stage stands on a floor. Your system has more floors than the proofs mention: a parser, a checker, solvers, a compiler, a runtime and a database. For each one you can say which it is: proved, validated per run, tested or trusted. Start with a floor you can add by accident.

choice.prompt: `native_decide` closes one IR golden. What joins your trusted base?

options.text: Nothing: the kernel still checks the proof.
options.why: `native_decide` has compiled code decide the goal, and the kernel does not evaluate it again.

options.text: The Lean compiler and its runtime.
options.why: Their output is trusted, and a native axiom appears in the list.
The kernel checks what `decide` does. It does not check `native_decide`.

blocks.md: The build stays green and the base has grown. `#print axioms` for such a goal names a native axiom, and the checker refuses it while its own log still says the kernel accepts the solution {{run:RUN-lean-axioms}}. That is SP-9.5, and the stamp is PROVED [P] · kernel + compiler.

You draw this table for your own system in LAB-9.12. Each row is a component, and its status says what stands behind it.

| Component | Status | What stands behind it |
|---|---|---|
| Lean kernel and its checkers | trusted | the comparator, and checkers that agree |
| Source semantics | trusted as the specification | goldens; never [P] |
| Parser and typechecker (Rust) | tested | [T] · n goldens |
| IR compiler (Lean) | proved | CL-9.2, with the kernel and any native axiom named |
| SQL compiler (Rust) | validated per run | CL-9.3, [T] · n or [M] · bound |
| SQL validator and its lifter | trusted, tested on mutants | the mutant suite |
| Runtime and retries (Rust) | tested; termination assumed | CL-6.1 [T], CL-6.5 [A] |
| PostgreSQL | trusted | SEAM-9 [A] |

Three claims sound like one. The command preserves your invariants (S4). The compiler preserves what the command means (CL-9.2 and CL-9.3). The runtime follows the target (S6 and S8). Each has its own method and stamp, and the chain is as strong as its weakest link. CompCert's own list of what it still trusts is this table, drawn by its authors: the semantics, the parser, assembler and linker, and the proof assistant.

A compiler can preserve meaning and still leak. S7's observer saw response bodies only. Compile the document view two ways, and compare two worlds that differ in tenant Birch's private documents.

blocks.direction: Pair asserts: W0 and W1 agree on everything Acme may know. The viewer runs both plans in both worlds, and shows frank's response and the steps each run took.

code.text:
view     Open(frank, doc) from S7, for tenant Acme
plan 1   full scan: read every document row, keep the ones frank may see
plan 2   index scan: read only the rows frank may see

W0       Acme's documents, and Birch's private ones
W1       W0 plus one more private document of Birch's

call.prompt: Both plans return the same body to frank in W0 and in W1. Can frank tell the worlds apart?

options.text: Yes, by the full scan's running time.
options.why: The full scan's step count includes Birch's private rows, and the index scan's does not.
CL-7.3's observer sees bodies only. Time lies outside it, as CompCert's observations leave time out.
The bodies are equal in both worlds.

blocks.after: The bodies match in both worlds, and the full scan's step count differs between them {{run:RUN-lean-leaky-compile}}. This is SP-9.6, an erosion: SEAM-10 cracks. The compiler preserved the observation you chose, and that observation omits time. Two remedies: widen the observer to include steps, which refutes CL-7.3 with this pair as [R], or state the timing channel as [N], choose the index plan, and claim only the observer you checked.

choice.prompt: Your SQL compiler emits a plan for every command, and your validator replays each plan on both semantics. What status does the compiler get in your base?

options.why: Nothing proves the compiler. Each plan is checked after it is made.
Trusting it would skip the per-plan check. The validator is what you trust here.

options.text: Tested: TESTED [T], from its unit tests alone.
options.why: The unit tests are evidence about the compiler. The per-plan replay is what CL-9.3 stands on.

options.text: Validated per run: [T] · n commands or [M] · bound.
options.why: The compiler stays untrusted, and the validator checks each plan it makes.

choice.prompt: Your report says: "a transfer that hits a serialization failure is retried until it commits." Which of the three claims does that sentence belong to?

options.why: That claim is about one command on the source, whatever the database does.
That claim is about what the compiled code means. Retries are about how it runs.
Retrying a failed transaction is the runtime's job, and its termination is assumed.

options.text: All three, since one proof covers the chain.
options.why: Each claim has its own method and stamp, and a proof of one says nothing about the next.

blocks.title: Production twin
blocks.md: Cedar tests its Lean specification against its Rust code by compiling the specification to C, so the Lean compiler joins Cedar's trusted base. AuthV2 trusts its DafnyLite compiler instead (ICSE 2025). At the `cedar-spec` commit pinned in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}, find where compiled Lean runs in the differential-testing harness.

blocks.title: Reading
blocks.md: CompCert manual, chapter 1, sections 1.2 and 1.3 (https://compcert.org/man/manual001.html, version pinned in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}), and Leroy, "Formal verification of a realistic compiler", CACM 2009, section 5, on what the compiler still trusts. Then Yang et al., "Finding and Understanding Bugs in C Compilers", PLDI 2011, section 3.1, on where Csmith found bugs in CompCert (read 2026-10-23).
